the three engines
engine 01

Apple CIRAWFilter

macOS's own Core Image raw engine. The fastest of the three, the broadest camera coverage, and the only path where Apple's raw noise reduction has any effect.

Adobe's own reference implementation, 1.7.1, compiled with JPEG XL. Every .dng goes through it unless you say otherwise.

Why we built a RAW developer that only runs on a Mac

[DATE]·7 MIN READ·[YOUR NAME]
Develop, with the tone controls open — one window for culling, developing and cataloguing.

Chili RAW started with a folder. Twelve hundred frames from a trip to Japan, sitting on a disk, and an afternoon gone before anyone reached the good ones — waiting for previews, waiting for a catalog to think about it, paying a monthly fee for the privilege. The editing was never the slow part. Everything around it was.

So we built the app we wanted: one window where a card full of frames becomes finished pictures. Cull, develop, catalogue, geotag, export. No import step, no round trip to a second app, and nothing sent anywhere.

One platform, and no baggage

Almost every photo application is written to run on Windows too, and it shows — its own rendering stack, its own widgets, its own idea of how a window should behave. Every one of those is a compromise, and you pay for all of them in speed.

Chili RAW runs on Apple silicon and nothing else. The develop pipeline is built on Metal and Core Image. The AI runs on the Neural Engine. The interface is native AppKit and SwiftUI. Dropping Intel and dropping Windows meant we could use what the platform actually offers, instead of the part that has an equivalent somewhere else.

Supporting one platform properly is a feature. It just doesn't look like one on a comparison chart.

Managing and developing, in the same window

Culling and developing are the same job done at different zoom levels, so they should not live in different applications — or in different modes that each forget what the other was doing. Rate a frame in the grid and open it in Develop; the rating, the stack it belongs to, the version you were working on, and the folder you came from all follow.

The catalog underneath is an index, not a vault. Your files stay in the folders you already have. Every edit is written to a small sidecar beside the photo, so nothing you make is trapped in a database only this app can open.

AI you can switch off and never meet again

The AI tools are genuinely useful — one click for a sky, a whole object removed, noise cleaned off a high-ISO frame. They are also completely optional, and we mean that more strictly than most apps do.

Chili RAW ships with no models at all. Nothing is downloaded until you press a button. Turn the master switch off in Settings and the AI controls are simply not there — no greyed-out temptations, no “upgrade to unlock”. There is no account, no telemetry, no analytics, and the only network request the app ever makes is fetching a model you asked for. If you want a RAW developer that never phones anywhere, that is exactly what you get by leaving one switch alone.

A film laboratory built for photographs

This is the part we built for ourselves. Experimenting with film looks is one of the reasons the app exists, and the tools for it are all aimed at motion — proper film pipelines with negative stock, print stock, halation and grain exist for colour grading video, and some of them cost several hundred to a thousand dollars. For photographs you usually get a LUT named after a film and nothing underneath it.

Film Labor is that pipeline, built for a single frame. Eighteen film stocks and eight papers, each modelled from the manufacturers' published measurements, run through the stages a real frame goes through: exposure onto the negative, halation, grain, the print, and the light you view it under. It is emulation rather than replication, and every stage can be switched off. LUTs are supported too, if that is all you want — but a LUT is a lookup table, and a lab is a sequence.

One price, or none at all

The free tier is a complete photo developer. Not a demo and not a countdown — the whole culling, developing and cataloguing workflow, including all three RAW decoders, with no time limit, no watermark, no nag screens and no account. For a lot of people it will be the whole story, and they will never need the paid part.

Pro adds what you make with the app rather than what you do to a file: Film Labor, the Pixels canvas, the on-device AI tools, and depth-based bokeh. It costs $29 while Chili RAW 1 is new, and $59 once version 1.5 ships — buy at the founding price and 1.5 is yours anyway, because a licence covers every 1.x build. Compare the two versions. One payment, not a subscription.

A new major version arrives about every eighteen months, and nobody is pushed onto it. The version you bought is yours for good — it keeps working, it keeps getting its 1.x updates, and moving to 2 is a decision you make when there is something in it you want. Future upgrades will be 25 USD, not full price again.

Chili RAW is built in the open, and the list of what it should do next is longer than the list of what it does. If something in it is wrong, or missing, or slower than it should be, tell us — the issue tracker is public and every report gets read.
